source.title: Transformers Can Learn Connectivity in Some Graphs but Not Others

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws in related work and reports scaling experiments, but those experiments concern supervised connectivity learning on synthetic graphs, not the language-model pretraining-loss or compute-allocation claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test loss and accuracy while varying model dimension, graph size, grid dimension, and chain count. These results are included as related scaling findings with versions ["none"]. It does not report held-out language-model pretraining loss, fitted power laws or exponents, extrapolations from smaller runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The Kaplan et al. result in related work is cited background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains small transformers on synthetic graph-connectivity classification and reports test loss/accuracy curves against FLOPs while varying embedding dimension and graph size. It fits no power laws, reports no exponents, makes no extrapolation, and does not measure language-model pretraining loss, compute-optimal allocation, shape effects at fixed parameters, or downstream tasks as a function of pretraining loss. Kaplan et al. appears only as related-work motivation. The results are task-specific generalization findings and do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that grid-graph performance stays consistent as graph size grows. They also conclude that data (graph-size) scaling benefits performance more than model scaling for higher-dimensional grids and for many-chain graphs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformers on synthetic graph-connectivity classification examples and measures task loss and accuracy while varying model or graph size. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported connectivity performance changes with graph topology, grid dimensionality, number of chains, graph size, and model embedding dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic connectivity tasks, larger embedding dimension lowers test loss on grid graphs but raises it on disconnected chains. Larger graphs (more training pairs) help higher-dimensional grids and many-chain graphs more than larger models do.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether model or data scaling improves generalization on a synthetic reasoning task depends on the task's structure; model scaling can increase test loss.

record.problems: The experiments concern synthetic graph tasks rather than language-model pretraining. Outcomes relevant to scaling are largely reported qualitatively in the text or visually in figures, without numerical test-loss values in the text. The paper reports ten random seeds and plots standard deviations.

untested.parts: Held-out LM pretraining loss and its power-law dependence on N, D or C.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count (depth is fixed at 4 layers).
Power-law form in other regimes; no fits are made even for the synthetic task.
Downstream performance versus scale or pretraining loss.

record.verdict_notes: Epoch counts differ across model and graph sizes (15000/10000/5000), so the curves are not matched on data passes. Test sets are tiny (about 40 positive plus negative pairs) and results are reported only in figures. No rows link to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or other training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: transformer

rows.operation_detail: Varied model embedding dimension and recorded test loss over training compute.
rows.value: figure only; text says test loss decreases as model size increases
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over ten random seeds are plotted; numeric uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper describes the overall trend across the model-size sweep; it does not give numerical test-loss values in the text.

rows.subject: transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic disconnected-chain connectivity examples
rows.operation_detail: Varied model embedding dimension and recorded test loss over training compute.
rows.value: figure only; text says test loss increases with model dimension
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over ten random seeds are plotted; numeric uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The paper states that model scaling increases test loss in this setting.
rows.check: Relative to the claim, 'reversed' is not meaningful. The row measures test loss on a synthetic classification task with no power-law fit. Within the study, test loss does rise with demb, and that should be kept as the row's descriptive value.

rows.subject: transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic grid-graph connectivity examples
rows.operation_detail: Varied graph node count and recorded test loss over training compute.
rows.value: figure only; text says test loss slightly decreases and performance remains consistent as graph size increases
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over ten random seeds are plotted; numeric uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The reported change in test loss is described as slight.
rows.check: The state is not defined against any version. Graph size conflates the number of training examples with task difficulty, so it is not a clean data-scaling measure.

rows.note: The paper reports the test-accuracy values approximately in the text.
